stories.brief: The ATA textile factory operated in Kfar Ata from 1934 to 1985, making clothing and household and industrial textiles that were sold through its own stores and other Israeli shops.

sources.title: Ata Textile Company LTD - Beit Fisher Archive
In Israel’s Textile Industry
ATA: Factory, Fashion and Dream
Fourteen-week Strike in Ata Textile Mills is Ended
2,000 Textile Works Are Dismissed

storyBeats: The Moller family, Jewish industrialists from Czechoslovakia, founded the ATA textile factory in Kfar Ata in 1934.
The factory made clothing and textiles for both household use and industry.
A 1955 study describes a production chain that began with raw cotton and included spinning, weaving, dyeing, finishing, sewing, and marketing.
The factory specialized in cotton goods, including cloth, shirts, trousers, underwear, raincoats, dresses, and children’s clothing.
ATA sold its products through other Israeli shops and businesses and through stores in its own chain.
In the 1955 study, the company had about 1,500 employees, 27 percent of them women, and operated a second factory called Kurdaneh in the Haifa Bay industrial zone.
Workers from the factory’s departments elected representatives to a central workers’ committee.
In 1957, a strike at ATA lasted about 14 weeks; its settlement included a pension fund and an annual bonus for workers.
The factory closed in 1985, and nearly 2,000 employees were told their jobs had ended.

stories.brief: The Shamouti orange, discovered in Jaffa’s orchards in the mid-19th century, became a major export; growers and traders packed the fruit carefully for long journeys to overseas markets.

sources.publisher: University of California, Riverside, Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection
sources.title: Shamouti sweet orange

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Agriculture, via AgEcon Search
sources.title: The Citrus Industry of Palestine
Jaffa Oranges
More Than Just Food: Shaping a National Identity Through Cuisine
Agriculture in Israel: Performance, Challenges, and Prospects

storyBeats: The Shamouti orange originated in an orchard near Jaffa before 1844 and became known in Europe as the Jaffa orange.
The fruit is oval, has a thick rind, and is nearly seedless; those qualities help it keep and travel well.
A mid-century agricultural study reported that the Shamouti had displaced other orange varieties around Jaffa by 1880.
The same study described the Shamouti as a mid-season fruit, picked from around mid-November and marketed from late November to about the end of April.
By the Mandate period, citrus was the leading agricultural industry and export, with Shamouti oranges especially prominent.
Growers shipped oranges through Jaffa’s port; Haifa also became an export port in the 1930s.
Exporters wrapped individual oranges in thin paper before placing them in crates to protect the fruit during long journeys.
The label “JAFFA ORANGES” appeared on the wrapping, and sometimes the name was marked directly on the fruit.
Although widely used as a shared identifying label, “JAFFA ORANGES” was not a registered trademark under local law.

stories.brief: In a letter from about 1792, Jewish woman Rebecca Samuel described her family’s planned move from Petersburg, Virginia, to Charleston, South Carolina, seeking a larger Jewish community while her husband earned a living as a watchmaker and silversmith.

sources.title: Letter from Rebecca Samuel to Her Parents
Rebecca Samuel
Modern Orthodox Judaism: A Documentary History

storyBeats: In a letter dated about 1792, Rebecca Samuel told her parents that her family planned to leave Petersburg, Virginia, for Charleston, South Carolina, after Passover.
Rebecca said the move was prompted by the small Jewish community in Petersburg, which she estimated at only ten or twelve people.
She described local Jewish religious life as limited: she said there was no Torah scroll for the High Holy Day services she recalled, and she longed for a synagogue to attend.
Rebecca wrote that Jewish shops in Petersburg opened on the Sabbath, while her own household kept its shop closed that day.
She stressed that the family was not leaving because of hostility or financial hardship; she said they could live peacefully and that her husband’s business was doing well.
Her husband Hyman worked as a watchmaker and made a clock that Rebecca praised for its accuracy.
Rebecca said Hyman spent more time making silverware than repairing watches and employed a skilled silversmith.
She described Petersburg as a busy tobacco-trading town, where large shipments arrived in hogsheads for onward trade.
Rebecca wanted her children to learn both Jewish and general subjects; she reported teaching her three-year-old daughter bedtime prayers and grace after meals.
Posen Library’s biographical note identifies Charleston as the destination Rebecca and her husband eventually chose and describes it as home to the largest Jewish community in America at that time.

stories.brief: The ATA textile factory operated in Kfar Ata from 1934 to 1985, making clothing and household and industrial textiles that were sold through its own stores and other Israeli shops.

sources.title: Ata Textile Company LTD - Beit Fisher Archive
In Israel’s Textile Industry
ATA: Factory, Fashion and Dream
Fourteen-week Strike in Ata Textile Mills is Ended
2,000 Textile Works Are Dismissed

storyBeats: The Moller family, Jewish industrialists from Czechoslovakia, founded the ATA textile factory in Kfar Ata in 1934.
The factory made clothing and textiles for both household use and industry.
A 1955 study describes a production chain that began with raw cotton and included spinning, weaving, dyeing, finishing, sewing, and marketing.
The factory specialized in cotton goods, including cloth, shirts, trousers, underwear, raincoats, dresses, and children’s clothing.
ATA sold its products through other Israeli shops and businesses and through stores in its own chain.
In the 1955 study, the company had about 1,500 employees, 27 percent of them women, and operated a second factory called Kurdaneh in the Haifa Bay industrial zone.
Workers from the factory’s departments elected representatives to a central workers’ committee.
In 1957, a strike at ATA lasted about 14 weeks; its settlement included a pension fund and an annual bonus for workers.
The factory closed in 1985, and nearly 2,000 employees were told their jobs had ended.

stories.brief: The Shamouti orange, discovered in Jaffa’s orchards in the mid-19th century, became a major export; growers and traders packed the fruit carefully for long journeys to overseas markets.

sources.publisher: University of California, Riverside, Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection
sources.title: Shamouti sweet orange

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Agriculture, via AgEcon Search
sources.title: The Citrus Industry of Palestine
Jaffa Oranges
More Than Just Food: Shaping a National Identity Through Cuisine
Agriculture in Israel: Performance, Challenges, and Prospects

storyBeats: The Shamouti orange originated in an orchard near Jaffa before 1844 and became known in Europe as the Jaffa orange.
The fruit is oval, has a thick rind, and is nearly seedless; those qualities help it keep and travel well.
A mid-century agricultural study reported that the Shamouti had displaced other orange varieties around Jaffa by 1880.
The same study described the Shamouti as a mid-season fruit, picked from around mid-November and marketed from late November to about the end of April.
By the Mandate period, citrus was the leading agricultural industry and export, with Shamouti oranges especially prominent.
Growers shipped oranges through Jaffa’s port; Haifa also became an export port in the 1930s.
Exporters wrapped individual oranges in thin paper before placing them in crates to protect the fruit during long journeys.
The label “JAFFA ORANGES” appeared on the wrapping, and sometimes the name was marked directly on the fruit.
Although widely used as a shared identifying label, “JAFFA ORANGES” was not a registered trademark under local law.

stories.brief: In a letter from about 1792, Jewish woman Rebecca Samuel described her family’s planned move from Petersburg, Virginia, to Charleston, South Carolina, seeking a larger Jewish community while her husband earned a living as a watchmaker and silversmith.

sources.title: Letter from Rebecca Samuel to Her Parents
Rebecca Samuel
Modern Orthodox Judaism: A Documentary History

storyBeats: In a letter dated about 1792, Rebecca Samuel told her parents that her family planned to leave Petersburg, Virginia, for Charleston, South Carolina, after Passover.
Rebecca said the move was prompted by the small Jewish community in Petersburg, which she estimated at only ten or twelve people.
She described local Jewish religious life as limited: she said there was no Torah scroll for the High Holy Day services she recalled, and she longed for a synagogue to attend.
Rebecca wrote that Jewish shops in Petersburg opened on the Sabbath, while her own household kept its shop closed that day.
She stressed that the family was not leaving because of hostility or financial hardship; she said they could live peacefully and that her husband’s business was doing well.
Her husband Hyman worked as a watchmaker and made a clock that Rebecca praised for its accuracy.
Rebecca said Hyman spent more time making silverware than repairing watches and employed a skilled silversmith.
She described Petersburg as a busy tobacco-trading town, where large shipments arrived in hogsheads for onward trade.
Rebecca wanted her children to learn both Jewish and general subjects; she reported teaching her three-year-old daughter bedtime prayers and grace after meals.
Posen Library’s biographical note identifies Charleston as the destination Rebecca and her husband eventually chose and describes it as home to the largest Jewish community in America at that time.
